passage: In the early days, people used the barter system, where goods were exchanged directly for other goods. This was often inefficient because it required a 'double coincidence of wants,' meaning both parties had to want exactly what the other offered. To solve this, money was introduced as a medium of exchange. Unlike ancient coins made of precious metals, modern paper currency has no intrinsic value; it is accepted because it is authorized by the government. The central authority, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), issues this currency on behalf of the central government. While the RBI manages the monetary system and supervises banks, it does not provide loans directly to the public, including small farmers. When individuals need credit, they approach commercial banks. To secure a loan, banks often require collateral, which is an asset—such as land, building, or vehicle—that the borrower owns and uses as a guarantee. This collateral is not a service fee; it remains the borrower's property unless they fail to repay the loan. If the borrower defaults, the bank has the right to sell the asset to recover the outstanding debt. Understanding these mechanisms helps individuals navigate the formal financial sector safely and effectively.

items.evidence: This was often inefficient because it required a 'double coincidence of wants,' meaning both parties had to want exactly what the other offered.
items.q: Ravi has many mangoes but the potter wants rice. Why does barter fail here?
options: The potter does not want what Ravi offers
Ravi does not have enough goods to trade
Ravi cannot save mangoes for a long time
Goods cannot be traded without a government
items.explain: Barter needs both people to want what the other offers; the potter wants rice, not mangoes.

wrong.why: thinks barter fails only for lack of goods
thinks exchange problems are about saving value

items.evidence: Unlike ancient coins made of precious metals, modern paper currency has no intrinsic value; it is accepted because it is authorized by the government.
items.q: Why do shopkeepers accept a ten-rupee paper note, though the paper is almost worthless?
options: The government has authorized it as money
The paper is made from precious metal
The note can be melted and sold
The note is worth its weight in gold
items.explain: Modern notes have no intrinsic value; people accept them because the government authorizes them.

wrong.why: thinks paper money has value like metal
thinks notes are valued by material worth
thinks notes are backed by gold content

items.evidence: While the RBI manages the monetary system and supervises banks, it does not provide loans directly to the public, including small farmers.
items.q: A small farmer needs a loan for seeds. Where should the farmer go?
options: To a commercial bank in the area
To the Reserve Bank of India office
To the central government's currency press
To the RBI's team that supervises banks
items.explain: The RBI does not lend to the public, so farmers approach commercial banks for credit.

wrong.why: thinks the RBI lends to farmers
confuses issuing currency with giving loans
thinks bank supervision includes lending to farmers

items.evidence: This collateral is not a service fee; it remains the borrower's property unless they fail to repay the loan.
items.q: Meena pledged her shop as collateral and repaid the whole loan. What happens to the shop?
options: It stays hers, as she did not default
The bank keeps it as a service fee
The bank keeps it as interest earned
It is sold to recover the bank's costs
items.explain: Collateral stays the borrower's property unless she fails to repay, so Meena keeps her shop.

wrong.why: thinks collateral is a fee paid to the bank
thinks lender keeps collateral even after repayment
thinks banks sell assets even without default
